name: Ju/'hoansi trance-healing tradition

dating.dating_summary: Documented via 20th-century ethnography (Marshall from the 1950s; Katz's fieldwork early-to-mid 1970s, published 1982; Biesele from the 1970s-90s) as a living practice; no independently dated time-depth for the specific institution as documented, though the general trickster-Mantis figure appears across many San groups' folklore per comparative work (Guenther 1999).

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: Rock art potentially depicting trance-dance postures exists but the link is a contested interpretive claim (Lewis-Williams/Dowson vs. Solomon), not confirmed continuity — see claim_rock_art_shamanism_disputed.

earliest_written_attestation.note: Lorna Marshall's Nyae Nyae fieldwork, published from 1959 onward, is the earliest substantial published ethnography of this specific group.

tradition_internal_claim.note: No single canonical origin narrative; described by practitioners as a longstanding living institution of "emotional, social, and moral balance" (Lee/Biesele framing).

notes: Richard Katz, Boiling Energy: Community Healing Among the Kalahari Kung (Harvard UP, 1982) — n/um ("energy") "boiling" during the all-night communal healing dance produces !kia/trance, enabling extraction of sickness; at dances Katz observed, roughly 1/4 of female singers and 2/3 of male dancers functioned as healers — both sexes participate, men a larger share of deep-trance healers. Megan Biesele, Women Like Meat (Witwatersrand UP/Indiana UP, 1993).
